blocks.title: How to use these
bullets: **Allow 45 minutes each.** Write the answers out; do not read ahead.
Each question is labelled with the chapter it draws on, **after** the answer, so the labels do not give the game away. Check which chapters you leaned on badly.
These are written to the pattern ICAI uses in Part I case scenarios and in the compulsory Q1 and Q5: one set of facts, several unrelated demands.

blocks.text: Cross-Chapter Case 1 — Mahanadi Ceramics Ltd. (Section A, five chapters)

blocks.title: Mahanadi Ceramics Ltd.
facts: Mahanadi Ceramics Ltd. makes sanitaryware at a single plant in Odisha and sells through 600 dealers. Its board is reviewing the year and a proposed expansion.

**Last year's results.** Sales ₹240 crore, all on 45 days' credit. Variable cost 55% of sales. Fixed operating cost ₹62 crore. Interest ₹18 crore on ₹150 crore of 12% debt. Tax 30%. Equity: 3 crore shares of ₹10, market price ₹95. Reserves ₹210 crore.
**The balance sheet position.** Inventory ₹48 crore, receivables ₹30 crore, cash ₹6 crore, current liabilities ₹40 crore (including creditors of ₹34 crore against annual purchases of ₹102 crore).

**The proposal.** A ₹120 crore second kiln, life 8 years, straight-line depreciation to nil, expected to add ₹60 crore of sales a year at the same variable-cost ratio and ₹14 crore of additional fixed operating cost. The board will fund it either entirely by 11% debentures or entirely by a rights issue at ₹80.

**The dividend question.** The company has paid ₹4 a share for six years. The finance director notes that the company's return on investment is 19% against a cost of equity of 14%, and asks whether the dividend should be maintained.

questions.q: Compute the operating, financial and combined leverage for last year, and say in one sentence what each tells the board.
a: **Contribution** = Sales − Variable cost = 240 − (55% × 240) = 240 − 132 = **₹108 crore**.
**EBIT** = Contribution − Fixed operating cost = 108 − 62 = **₹46 crore**. **EBT** = EBIT − Interest = 46 − 18 = **₹28 crore**.
**Operating leverage = Contribution ÷ EBIT = 108 ÷ 46 = 2.35 times.** A 1% change in sales moves EBIT by 2.35%, and the cause is the ₹62 crore of fixed operating cost.
**Financial leverage = EBIT ÷ EBT = 46 ÷ 28 = 1.64 times.** A 1% change in EBIT moves EPS by 1.64%, and the cause is the ₹18 crore interest commitment.
**Combined leverage = Contribution ÷ EBT = 108 ÷ 28 = 3.86 times** (or 2.35 × 1.64). A 1% change in sales moves EPS by 3.86%.

**What it tells the board:** total risk is high. A 10% sales fall would cut EPS by about 39%, and roughly three-fifths of that sensitivity is operating rather than financial — so the first lever is the cost structure, not the debt.
*Chapter: FM 6 Leverages.*

questions.q: Compute the operating cycle and the net operating cycle in days, and state why the difference matters.
a: **Inventory holding period.** Cost of goods sold ≈ variable cost + fixed operating cost = 132 + 62 = ₹194 crore. Inventory ₹48 crore ÷ 194 × 365 ≈ **90 days**.
**Receivables period.** Given as 45 days' credit; check: 30 ÷ 240 × 365 ≈ **46 days** — consistent, so collections are on terms.
**Operating cycle = 90 + 46 = 136 days.**
**Creditors period.** 34 ÷ 102 × 365 ≈ **122 days**.
**Net operating cycle = 136 − 122 = 14 days.**

**Why the difference matters:** the gross cycle of 136 days is what the business ties up in operations; the net cycle of 14 days is what the **company itself has to fund**, because suppliers are financing 122 days of it. The company looks comfortable on that measure — but a 122-day creditors period against purchases is unusually long, and if suppliers tightened to 60 days the net cycle would jump to roughly 76 days and the funding requirement with it. That dependence is the real finding.
*Chapter: FM 9 Management of Working Capital.*

questions.q: Appraise the kiln on NPV at a 14% discount rate, and state the single assumption that most affects your answer.
a: **Incremental contribution** = 60 × (1 − 0.55) = **₹27 crore** a year. Less additional fixed operating cost ₹14 crore → **incremental EBITDA ₹13 crore**.

**Depreciation** = 120 ÷ 8 = **₹15 crore** a year. So incremental EBIT = 13 − 15 = **−₹2 crore**, and the tax effect is a **saving** of 0.30 × 2 = ₹0.6 crore (assuming the loss is absorbed against other profits, which it can be here).
**Annual cash flow after tax** = EBIT after tax + depreciation = (−2 + 0.6) + 15 = **₹13.6 crore**.

**The assumption that dominates:** the ₹60 crore of additional sales. At the given cost structure the kiln needs roughly ₹120 crore of extra sales a year to break even on NPV — double what is projected. Before rejecting, the board should test whether the ₹60 crore is a first-year figure that grows, and whether any terminal value attaches to the kiln after year 8, since the appraisal assumes it is worthless.

**Note what the depreciation does and does not do.** It is not a cash flow, so it is added back; but it does shelter tax, which is why it appears twice in the working. Treating it as a cash outflow is the commonest error in this question.
*Chapter: FM 7 Investment Decisions.*

questions.q: Compute the EPS under each funding route and find the indifference point. Which route should the board prefer?
a: **New EBIT** = 46 + 13 = **₹59 crore** (existing EBIT plus incremental EBITDA), less the new depreciation of ₹15 crore → **₹44 crore**.
**Debenture route.** Interest = 18 + (11% × 120) = 18 + 13.2 = ₹31.2 crore. EBT = 44 − 31.2 = ₹12.8 crore; PAT = 8.96 crore; shares 3 crore. **EPS = ₹2.99.**
**Rights route.** New shares = 120 ÷ 80 = 1.5 crore, total 4.5 crore. Interest stays ₹18 crore. EBT = 44 − 18 = ₹26 crore; PAT = ₹18.2 crore. **EPS = ₹4.04.**

**The decision.** Expected EBIT after the project is ₹44 crore, which is **below** the ₹57.6 crore indifference point, so the **equity (rights) route gives the higher EPS** — as the computation confirms, ₹4.04 against ₹2.99.

**But note the prior question.** The project's NPV is negative, so the better advice is not to choose a funding route at all. If it proceeds, equity; and the board should notice that the debt route would push financial leverage from 1.64 to 44 ÷ 12.8 = **3.44 times**, on a business whose operating leverage is already 2.35.
*Chapters: FM 5 Capital Structure and FM 6 Leverages.*

questions.q: Should the ₹4 dividend be maintained? Answer using Walter's model.
a: **Walter's model** holds that the payout decision follows from the relationship between the firm's return on investment (r) and its cost of equity (Ke). Here **r = 19% and Ke = 14%, so r > Ke** — a **growth firm**.

**For a growth firm the optimum payout is nil.** Every rupee retained earns 19% inside the company against the 14% shareholders require, so retention adds to the market price and distribution subtracts from it.
**So on Walter's logic the dividend should be cut to nil**, and the model says the price would be higher for it.

**What the model leaves out, and why a board would hesitate.** Walter assumes r and Ke are constant and that retained earnings are the only financing; both fail here, since the company is simultaneously considering a rights issue. More practically, a dividend paid for six consecutive years carries an **informational content** — cutting it signals distress — and the study material's determinants of dividend policy include shareholder expectations and the stability of dividends. A defensible answer: Walter's model indicates retention, but the realistic recommendation is to **hold the ₹4 and fund the expansion from the rights issue**, which is what the EPS comparison also supports.
*Chapter: FM 8 Dividend Decisions.*

blocks.takeaway: Five chapters, one set of facts, and the answers interact: the leverage computation explains why the debt route is risky, the NPV says the project should not proceed at all, and the dividend answer has to be reconciled with the rights issue being considered in the funding question. That interaction is what a chapter test cannot teach you.

blocks.text: Cross-Chapter Case 2 — Nilgiri Organics Ltd. (Section B, all five chapters)

blocks.title: Nilgiri Organics Ltd.
facts: Nilgiri Organics Ltd. grows and packs organic tea and spices in the Nilgiris, sells through modern trade in six Indian cities, and exports a little to the Gulf. A new managing director has been appointed and has a year to produce a plan.

**The founder's firm.** The company was built over eighteen years by a founder who personally approved every supplier and refused to sell to any retailer who would not display the produce unrefrigerated. Staff still quote him. The written strategy is one page long and has not changed since 2019.

**The outside world.** Two national FMCG groups have launched organic ranges at 20% below Nilgiri's prices. A new state regulation will require farm-level traceability certification within two years. Consumer research shows buyers of organic produce are younger than the company assumes and buy mostly online. A tea-pest outbreak in a neighbouring district has raised input prices 30% in four months.

**Inside.** Nilgiri's eleven-year-old relationship with 400 certified farmers, and the soil-management protocol it taught them, let it certify produce in three weeks where rivals take three months. Two competitors have tried to copy the protocol by hiring its agronomists and have not matched it. Its packing plant is ordinary. Its brand is strong in two cities and unknown in the other four.

**The choices on the table.** (1) Sell the same packs harder in the six cities. (2) Enter eight new cities with the same range. (3) Launch a ready-to-drink iced tea for the existing cities. (4) Buy a spice-grinding unit that currently processes Nilgiri's produce. (5) Buy a loss-making organic dairy in another state. (6) Shut the Gulf export desk, which has lost money for three years after a turnaround attempt failed.

**And the organisation.** The company is organised by function under the managing director. Nobody owns the online channel. The plan will require farm traceability software at 400 farms, and the field officers who must deploy it have never used a smartphone for work.

questions.q: Classify the outside facts using the right SM Chapter 2 tools, and say which force or element each belongs to.
a: **The macro environment, through PESTLE.** The traceability regulation is **legal-regulatory** (and arguably political). The shift to younger, online buyers is **socio-cultural**. The pest outbreak raising input prices 30% is **environmental**, feeding through to **economic**.

**The industry environment, through Porter's five forces.** The two national FMCG groups launching organic ranges at 20% below Nilgiri's prices are **new entrants** — the force is named from the incumbent's position, and their arrival shows the entry barriers are low for a group with distribution and brand. Their pricing then raises **rivalry**. The pest outbreak raises **supplier bargaining power** over the input. Modern-trade retailers who can delist the range hold **buyer bargaining power**.
**Product life cycle.** Organic produce in India is in the **growth** stage — which is precisely why national groups are entering, and why rivalry is about share rather than survival.

**The method point:** do not force every fact into one tool. The study material's own structure is macro environment first (PESTLE), then industry (five forces), then product and market — and a fact can appear in more than one, as the pest outbreak does.
*Chapter: SM 2 Strategic Analysis: External Environment.*

questions.q: Is the farmer relationship and soil protocol a core competency? Apply the study material's own criteria.
a: **Yes, and the facts are built to satisfy each criterion.** Prahalad and Hamel's three areas: **customer value** — three-week certification against three months is a benefit the customer can see, in freshness and availability; **competitor differentiation** — two competitors have tried to copy it and failed, which is the test of competitive uniqueness; **application to other markets** — the protocol would transfer to any crop the 400 farmers could grow, which is what makes choices (3) and (4) credible.

**Why the copying attempt failed, and why that matters.** The rivals hired the agronomists and still could not match the result, which tells you the competency is not in the individuals but in the **relationship and the accumulated practice** — eleven years of it. That is the difference between a resource and a capability, and it is what makes the competency **sustainable**.

**Contrast the packing plant.** It is ordinary, so it is a resource but not a competency. And the brand is a competency in two cities only — which bears directly on whether choice (2), entering eight new cities, can lean on it.
*Chapter: SM 3 Strategic Analysis: Internal Environment.*

questions.q: Classify the six choices on the right frameworks, and recommend which to pursue first.
a: **(1) Same packs, same six cities → market penetration.** Existing product, existing market; achieved by more sales to present customers without changing the product in any major way.
**(2) Same range, eight new cities → market development.** Existing product, new market, through new geographical markets.

**(3) Ready-to-drink iced tea for existing cities → product development.** New product, existing market. Under §4.2.2.3 it is also **concentric diversification**, linked through process, technology and marketing.

**(4) Buying the spice-grinding unit that already processes Nilgiri's produce → backward integration**, a form of vertically integrated diversification: the creation of effective supply by entering the business of input providers.

**(5) Buying a loss-making organic dairy in another state → conglomerate diversification** — and a poor one. No common thread in technology or the farmer network, and the target is loss-making, so the firm would be buying a turnaround it has no competency to run.

**(6) Shutting the Gulf export desk after a failed turnaround → divestment**, on ICAI's own sequencing: 'adopted when a turnaround has been attempted but has proved to be unsuccessful'. If no buyer exists and the desk is simply closed, it is **liquidation**.

**The recommendation, and the reason.** Do **(6)** immediately — it releases management attention and cash, and the condition for divestment is already satisfied. Then **(3) product development** and **(4) backward integration**, because both are built on the competency the previous answer established: the iced tea uses the same certified leaf, and the grinding unit protects the input the pest outbreak has just made precarious. **(1) penetration** is the cheapest growth and should run alongside. Defer **(2)**, because the brand is unknown in four of the six cities it already serves and market development without a brand is an expensive way to discover that. Reject **(5)** outright.
*Chapter: SM 4 Strategic Choices.*

questions.q: The founder's culture conflicts with the plan. Diagnose the problem and set out how the new MD should handle the organisation and the technology rollout.
a: **The culture.** Corporate culture is a company's **values, beliefs, business principles, traditions, ways of operating, and internal work environment**, and Nilgiri's is unusually legible: the founder's personal supplier approval, the unrefrigerated-display rule, and the fact that **staff still quote him** — the study material's point that culture emerges from **the stories that get told over and over again**. Culture is **either an important contributor or an obstacle**; the refusal to sell to retailers who will not display unrefrigerated is now an obstacle to online selling, which is where the buyers are.

**Which side gives way.** Usually **revamping the mismatched cultural features to produce strategy fit** rather than the reverse — but the strategy maker must **select a strategy compatible with the 'sacred' or unchangeable parts** of the culture. Here the sacred part is the produce quality the display rule was meant to protect; the rule itself is not sacred. So change the rule and keep the standard. Expect it to take time: in large companies significant culture change takes **two to five years**.

**The structure.** Functional under the MD, with **nobody owning the online channel** — and online is where the plan's growth is. ICAI's **symptoms of an ineffective structure** include too much attention to interdepartmental conflict and too many unachieved objectives. The remedy is a **divisional structure by customer** (modern trade against online), which 'allows an organization to cater effectively to the requirements of clearly defined customer groups'. Note Chandler both ways: **structure should follow strategy**, but a strategy needing massive structural change is itself less attractive.

**The technology rollout.** Traceability software at 400 farms with field officers who have never used a smartphone for work is a **change management** problem, not an IT problem. Use §5.3.3's five best practices: **begin at the top**; **ensure the change is both necessary and desired** — here the regulation makes it necessary, which is a gift; **reduce disruption** by getting the word out early, giving the officers the knowledge and tools, and empowering change agents; **encourage communication**; and **recognise that change is the norm**. Then run it on §5.3.4's pointers: specify the aims, communicate always, **be ready for resistance**, **implement gradually** rather than at 400 farms at once, and **offer assistance and training**.

**The leadership style.** A poorly performing firm in a turbulent environment facing major change is the study material's own setting for **transformational** leadership — charisma and vision to elicit dramatic change — while the packing plant and the certification protocol, which work, should be run **transactionally**.
*Chapter: SM 5 Strategy Implementation and Evaluation.*

questions.q: What controls and measures should the MD install, and what does the one-page 2019 strategy tell you?
a: **The 2019 strategy document is the diagnosis.** A strategy unchanged for six years, in a market where regulation, buyer demographics, input prices and competition have all moved, is a **premise control** failure: a strategy is built on **certain assumptions or premises about the complex and turbulent organizational environment**, and **over a period of time these premises may not remain valid**. Nobody checked.

**Premise control** should now monitor, by name, the assumptions the plan rests on: the traceability regulation (**legal-regulatory**), input prices (**economic**), and the national groups' pricing (**industry — competitors**). ICAI's selectivity point applies: **it is neither feasible nor desirable to control all types of premises in the same manner**, so pick the ones likely to change and likely to hurt.
**Strategic surveillance** — deliberately **unfocussed, casual environmental browsing** — is what would have caught the demographic shift to younger online buyers before the research did.

**Special alert control** for the shock: a further pest outbreak, or an acquisition among the national groups, would **trigger an immediate and intense review of strategy**, handled by a **crisis management team**.

**Implementation control** for the plan itself, in both forms: **monitoring strategic thrusts** on the traceability rollout, and **milestone reviews** at the 100th, 250th and 400th farm, each involving **a complete reassessment**.

**And measures, because control needs standards.** The company almost certainly reports financial measures only. It needs **customer satisfaction measures** (retention, complaints), **market measures** (share in each of the six cities and the online channel), **employee measures** (field-officer attrition during the rollout) and **innovation measures** (the iced-tea launch). Choose them on **relevance, data availability, data quality and data timeliness**, remembering that **KPIs will influence the behaviour of people within the organisation** — a raw certification-speed target would push the field officers to cut the very protocol that is the competency.
*Chapter: SM 5 Strategy Implementation and Evaluation.*

blocks.takeaway: This case is the whole of Section B in one company, and the answers are chained: the external analysis establishes the threat, the internal analysis establishes what the firm can answer it with, the strategic choices follow from that competency, and the implementation answer is constrained by the culture the founder built. Note that the single most damaging fact in the case — a strategy document unchanged since 2019 — is a Chapter 5 control failure, not a Chapter 2 or 4 one.

blocks.title: SM Case Scenario — Sarayu Foods Ltd.
facts: Sarayu Foods Ltd., a listed company with its head office in Lucknow, runs three businesses: packaged spices (₹900 crore of revenue, growing at 4% a year in a market growing at 3%, where Sarayu is the clear leader), ready-to-cook frozen food (₹160 crore, growing at 38% in a market growing at 40%, where Sarayu is third of seven players) and a nine-month-old range of millet health bars (₹12 crore, in a market nobody can yet size).

The board has just finished a two-day retreat. The managing director opened it by asking the group heads to decide which of the three businesses the company is going to be, and how the company's money should be split between them — not how any one of them should be run.

In spices, the top three brands hold 71% of the market between them; the remaining share is held by unbranded local millers who sell loose spice at roughly 40% below Sarayu's price. Packaging film, Sarayu's largest bought-in input, comes from two suppliers nationally. The large modern-trade chains that take 34% of Sarayu's spice volume renegotiate terms every year and have begun launching their own private-label spice lines.

Sarayu's frozen food business wins on one thing: a cold chain that holds −18°C from factory to shelf in a country where the rest of the trade cannot. It costs more to run than rivals' and Sarayu charges a 22% premium for it to urban households who will pay for food that has not been through a thaw cycle.

The company is organised as three self-contained units, each with its own manufacturing, sales force, marketing budget and profit-and-loss account, each headed by a chief executive who reports to the managing director, with group finance, legal and human resources held at the centre.

blocks.text: Mark your own paper before you read the explanations. Give yourself the full marks for a part only if your **working** reaches the answer — a right figure with no working earns part marks in the exam and a wrong figure with right working earns most of them.
Part I — Answer key with reasons

rows: DOL = Contribution ÷ EBIT. Contribution = 1,200 − 720 = ₹480 lakh; EBIT = 480 − 280 = ₹200 lakh; DOL = 480 ÷ 200 = **2.40**. (A) is the DFL; (C) is the combined leverage.
A change in sales moves EPS through the **combined** leverage: DCL = DOL × DFL = 2.40 × 1.3333 = 3.20. EPS change = 10% × 3.20 = **32%**. (B) uses DOL alone — the trap.
Quick assets = 400 − 160 = ₹240 lakh; ÷ current liabilities ₹160 lakh = **1.50 : 1**. (C) is the current ratio.
PAT = (200 − 50) × 0.75 = ₹112.5 lakh. Shareholders' funds = 100 + 300 = ₹400 lakh. ROE = **28.13%**. (A) is EPS in rupees; (B) is ROCE on ₹900 lakh.
Financial break-even is the EBIT that exactly covers the fixed financial charge. With no preference capital, that is the interest of **₹50 lakh**, at which PBT and hence EPS is nil.
Ke = Rf + β(Rm − Rf) = 7 + 1.4 (13 − 7) = 7 + 8.4 = **15.40%**. (C) wrongly uses β × Rm; (D) adds Rf to β × Rm.
Gross operating cycle = 45 + 15 + 30 + 60 = 150 days; less payment period 50 = **100 days**. (C) is the gross cycle — the trap.
A **deep discount bond** is a long-term instrument and belongs to the capital market. Commercial paper, certificates of deposit and treasury bills all mature within a year.
Which businesses to be in, and how to allocate resources between them, is the defining question of **corporate-level** strategy. Business level asks how to compete within one of them.

Annual renegotiation plus the credible threat of backward integration into private label is textbook **buyer power**. The two-supplier packaging film would be supplier power — a different fact in the same scenario.

Sarayu charges a 22% premium, serves urban households generally and accepts a higher cost to deliver an attribute rivals cannot match: **differentiation**. It is not focused — no narrow segment is named.

Spices: high relative market share, 3% market growth → **cash cow**. Frozen food: 40% market growth but third of seven, so low relative share → **question mark**. The 38% own growth rate tempts you to call it a star; BCG uses *relative market share*, not own growth.

Three self-contained businesses, each with its own functions and P&L and a chief executive reporting to the MD, with group functions at the centre, is an **SBU structure**. A divisional structure would not normally give each unit its own complete set of functions and a chief executive of its own.

A notified mandatory labelling requirement is a **legal** factor — the law as it binds the company. Environmental covers the physical environment and resource constraints; the deposit-refund purpose is environmental, but the factor the company must respond to is the statute.
High power, low interest → **keep satisfied**. Low power low interest = minimal effort; low power high interest = keep informed; high power high interest = key player.
**Strategic surveillance** is the broad, unfocused watch. (A) is premise control, (C) is special alert control, (D) is implementation control.

blocks.label: Q1(a) — Godavari Pipes Ltd., NPV and PI
blocks.question: COMPUTE the net present value and the profitability index of the ₹30,00,000 machine, and ADVISE the company.
answer_points: **Step 2 — EBIT.** Contribution ₹20,00,000 − cash fixed cost ₹6,00,000 − depreciation (₹30,00,000 ÷ 5) ₹6,00,000 = **₹8,00,000**.
**Step 4 — annual cash inflow.** PAT ₹5,60,000 + depreciation ₹6,00,000 = **₹11,60,000**. Depreciation is added back because it is a non-cash charge; it was deducted only to get the tax shield right.
blocks.conclusion: The NPV is positive at ₹11,81,800 and the PI exceeds 1. The machine should be purchased.
blocks.marks_split: 1 mark for the cash flow computation, 1 for the depreciation add-back, 1 for the PV, 1 for the NPV, 1 for the PI and the advice.
blocks.mistake: Forgetting to add depreciation back, which understates every year's cash flow by ₹6,00,000 and turns the NPV negative. The other half of the same mistake is omitting depreciation from the EBIT line, which overstates the tax by ₹1,80,000 a year.

blocks.label: Q1(b) — Narmada Ceramics Ltd., WACC
blocks.question: CALCULATE the weighted average cost of capital using book value weights.
answer_points: **Cost of equity (dividend growth model).** Ke = (D1 ÷ P0) + g = (3 ÷ 25) + 0.03 = 0.12 + 0.03 = **15%**.
**Cost of debentures.** Kd = 10% × (1 − 0.30) = **7%**.
**Weights (book value).** Equity funds = share capital ₹50,00,000 + reserves ₹30,00,000 = ₹80,00,000; debentures ₹40,00,000; term loan ₹30,00,000. Total ₹1,50,00,000.
**Reserves carry the cost of equity.** They belong to the equity shareholders and are not free. Leaving them out is the single most common error in this question.
blocks.conclusion: The weighted average cost of capital on book value weights is 11.55%.
blocks.marks_split: 1 mark each for Ke, Kd and Kt; 1 for the weights including reserves; 1 for the weighted total.
blocks.mistake: Using the market price ₹25 to weight the equity when the question says book value weights, and omitting reserves from the equity weight. Note also that the ₹25 price is needed for Ke even though it is not used as a weight — the question gives it for that reason, not as a trap.
topics: FM Ch 4 §9 Weighted Average Cost of Capital
FM Ch 4 §7 Cost of Equity Share Capital

blocks.label: Q1(c) — Kosi Components Ltd., working capital requirement
blocks.question: PREPARE a statement of working capital requirement.
answer_points: **Monthly cost figures.** Raw material 60,000 × ₹40 ÷ 12 = ₹2,00,000; labour 60,000 × ₹20 ÷ 12 = ₹1,00,000; overheads 60,000 × ₹15 ÷ 12 = ₹75,000. Total cost per month ₹3,75,000.

**Current assets.** Raw material stock (1 month) ₹2,00,000. Work in process (½ month, raw material full, labour and overheads half): 2,00,000 × ½ + 1,00,000 × ¼ + 75,000 × ¼ = 1,00,000 + 25,000 + 18,750 = **₹1,43,750**. Finished goods (1 month at total cost) ₹3,75,000. Debtors (2 months at cost) ₹7,50,000. Cash ₹50,000. **Total current assets ₹15,18,750.**
**Current liabilities.** Creditors for raw material (1½ months) 2,00,000 × 1.5 = ₹3,00,000. Outstanding wages (½ month) 1,00,000 × ½ = ₹50,000. **Total current liabilities ₹3,50,000.**

**Why labour and overheads are taken at half in work in process.** Raw material is issued in full at the start of processing, so a unit in process carries its whole material cost; labour and overheads accrue evenly over the half month, so on average a unit in process has absorbed half of them.
blocks.conclusion: Net working capital requirement = ₹15,18,750 − ₹3,50,000 = ₹11,68,750.
blocks.marks_split: 1 mark for the monthly cost base, 1 for work in process, 1 for finished goods and debtors, 1 for current liabilities, 1 for the net figure.
blocks.mistake: Valuing debtors at the selling price of ₹100 when the question says at cost — that alone adds ₹2,50,000 to the answer. The second is taking raw material at half in work in process along with labour and overheads.
topics: FM Ch 9 §5 Estimating Working Capital Needs
FM Ch 9 §6.1 Working Capital Based on Operating Cycle

blocks.label: Q2(a) — Bhima Engineering Ltd., the three leverages
blocks.question: CALCULATE DOL, DFL and DCL, and STATE the effect of a 15% fall in sales on earnings before tax.
answer_points: **Effect of a 15% fall in sales.** EBT falls by 15% × 3.11 = **46.67%**, that is by ₹2,10,000, leaving EBT of ₹2,40,000. Check: contribution falls to ₹11,90,000, EBIT to ₹3,90,000, EBT to ₹2,40,000. ✓
blocks.conclusion: A 15% fall in sales costs the company 46.67% of its pre-tax profit — the price of a cost structure in which ₹8,00,000 of operating cost and ₹1,50,000 of interest are both fixed.
blocks.marks_split: 1 mark each for contribution, EBIT and EBT; 1 for the three ratios; 1 for the percentage effect with a check.
blocks.mistake: Applying DOL to get the effect on EBT. DOL gives the effect on EBIT; the effect on EBT (and on EPS) needs the combined leverage.

blocks.label: Q2(b) — Ghaggar Tools Ltd., EPS indifference point
blocks.question: COMPUTE the EBIT at which EPS under the two plans would be the same, and ADVISE the company if EBIT is expected to be ₹50,00,000.
answer_points: **Shares under each plan.** Plan A: 10,00,000 existing + 5,00,000 new = **15,00,000 shares**, no debt. Plan B: 10,00,000 + 2,50,000 = **12,50,000 shares**, plus ₹50,00,000 of 12% debentures carrying interest of ₹6,00,000.
**The indifference equation.** EPS(A) = EPS(B), so (EBIT × 0.70) ÷ 15,00,000 = [(EBIT − 6,00,000) × 0.70] ÷ 12,50,000.

**Cancel the tax factor** (0.70 appears on both sides) and cross-multiply, working in lakhs of shares: 12.5 × EBIT = 15 × (EBIT − 6,00,000) → 12.5 EBIT = 15 EBIT − 90,00,000 → 2.5 EBIT = 90,00,000 → **EBIT = ₹36,00,000**.
blocks.conclusion: The expected EBIT of ₹50,00,000 is well above the indifference level of ₹36,00,000, so the debt-bearing Plan B gives the higher EPS (₹2.46 against ₹2.33) and should be preferred — subject to the company's willingness to carry the added financial risk.
blocks.marks_split: 1 mark for the share counts, 1 for setting up the equation, 1 for the indifference EBIT, 1 for the verification, 1 for the advice at ₹50,00,000.
blocks.mistake: Taking 5,00,000 and 2,50,000 as the total number of shares instead of adding them to the 10,00,000 already in issue. Also: issuing shares of ₹10 at a premium of ₹10 means ₹20 per share, so ₹1,00,00,000 needs 5,00,000 shares, not 10,00,000.
topics: FM Ch 6 §4.1 Degree of Financial Leverage

blocks.label: Q3(a) — Sutlej Agro Ltd., Walter's model
blocks.question: DETERMINE the market price per share at payout ratios of 0%, 50% and 100%, and COMMENT.
answer_points: **The formula.** P = [D + (r ÷ Ke) (E − D)] ÷ Ke, where E = ₹12, r = 14%, Ke = 12%.

**Reading the pattern.** The price falls as the payout rises. Walter's model says this happens whenever **r > Ke**: every rupee retained earns 14% inside the company against the 12% the shareholder requires, so retention adds value and distribution destroys it.
blocks.conclusion: For Sutlej Agro Ltd., r (14%) exceeds Ke (12%), so it is a growth firm and the optimum payout under Walter's model is **nil** — the share is worth most, ₹116.67, when nothing is distributed.
blocks.marks_split: ½ mark for the formula, 1 mark for each of the three computations, 1½ marks for the r versus Ke comment and the optimum payout.
blocks.mistake: Writing the comment the other way round. The rule is: r > Ke → zero payout (growth firm); r < Ke → 100% payout (declining firm); r = Ke → payout is irrelevant (normal firm).
topics: FM Ch 8 §8.2 Dividend's Relevance Theory (Walter's model)

blocks.label: Q3(b) — Pennar Castings Ltd., ratios in reverse
blocks.question: COMPUTE current assets, current liabilities and inventory, and EXPLAIN what the gap between the two ratios tells a lender.
answer_points: **Set up.** Let current liabilities = x. Current assets = 3x. Working capital = CA − CL = 3x − x = 2x = ₹3,00,000.
**Current assets.** 3x = **₹4,50,000**.
**Inventory.** Current assets − quick assets = ₹4,50,000 − ₹2,62,500 = **₹1,87,500**.

**What the gap says.** A current ratio of 3 looks comfortable, but ₹1,87,500 of the ₹4,50,000 — 41.7% of current assets — is inventory, which converts to cash only after it is sold and then collected. The quick ratio of 1.75 is the ratio that matters to a lender asked to be repaid next month.
blocks.conclusion: CA ₹4,50,000, CL ₹1,50,000, inventory ₹1,87,500. The company is liquid on both measures, but the 1.25-point gap between the two ratios shows that its liquidity is substantially tied up in stock, and a lender would ask how fast that stock turns before relying on the current ratio.
blocks.marks_split: 2 marks for CA and CL, 1 for quick assets, 1 for inventory, 1 for the interpretation.
blocks.mistake: Treating working capital as equal to current assets. Working capital is the *difference* between current assets and current liabilities; the whole solution turns on that one line.

blocks.label: Q4 — theory (4 + 4 + 2)
blocks.question: (a) The three financial decisions and why wealth maximisation beats profit maximisation. (b) Trading on equity. (c) Business risk versus financial risk / MM assumptions.
answer_points: **(a) The three decisions.** *Financing decision* — how much to raise and in what mix of debt and equity, so as to reach the capital structure with the lowest weighted average cost of capital. *Investment decision* — where to commit the funds, covering both long-term capital budgeting and the short-term working capital decision. *Dividend decision* — how much of the earnings to distribute and how much to retain, which is also the decision on internally generated finance.

**(a) Why wealth maximisation is the better objective.** Profit maximisation is vague (profit before or after tax, short run or long run); it ignores the **timing** of the returns, treating a rupee earned in year five as equal to one earned today; it ignores the **risk** attaching to those returns; and it can be achieved by cutting research, maintenance or quality, which raises this year's profit and lowers the value of the firm. Wealth maximisation uses the **present value of expected future cash flows discounted at a rate that reflects their risk**, and so answers all three objections.

**(b) Trading on equity.** The use of fixed-cost sources of finance — debt and preference capital — in the capital structure so as to raise the return to the equity shareholders. It works because the fixed charge is limited and tax-deductible: once the fixed charge is covered, the whole of the additional return belongs to the equity.

**(b) When it helps and when it hurts.** It works **for** the equity shareholders when the rate of return on the capital employed exceeds the rate of interest on the debt, so the surplus accrues to the equity, and when earnings are stable enough to cover the fixed charge comfortably. It works **against** them when the return on capital employed falls below the cost of debt — the shortfall is borne entirely by the equity — and when earnings are volatile, since the fixed charge must be met in a bad year too. The leverage magnifies losses exactly as it magnifies gains.

**(c) Business risk versus financial risk.** *Business risk* arises from the firm's operations and its operating cost structure; it exists even in a debt-free firm, is measured by the degree of operating leverage, and is created by the fixed operating costs. *Financial risk* arises from the use of debt and preference capital; it exists only if the firm uses fixed-cost finance, is measured by the degree of financial leverage, and is created by the fixed financial charges. Business risk is largely given by the industry the firm is in; financial risk is chosen by the board.

**(c) OR — four MM assumptions.** (i) Capital markets are perfect: information is free, investors behave rationally and securities are infinitely divisible. (ii) There are no transaction costs and no flotation costs. (iii) Investors can borrow and lend on the same terms as firms. (iv) There are no taxes (in the original 1958 propositions) and firms can be grouped into homogeneous risk classes. A further assumption is a 100% dividend payout, so that there are no retained earnings.
blocks.marks_split: (a) 2 marks for the three decisions, 2 for the four grounds of comparison. (b) 2 marks for the concept, 2 for the two sets of conditions. (c) 2 marks for any three well-stated points of distinction, or any four assumptions.
blocks.mistake: In (a), listing the three decisions and stopping. The marks for the second half come from naming vagueness, timing, risk and the scope for manipulation as four *separate* grounds — not from a general statement that wealth maximisation is "better in the long run".
topics: FM Ch 6 §4.2 Financial Leverage as Trading on Equity

blocks.text: Part II — Section B (SM) model answers

blocks.label: Q5(a) — Vaigai Hospitality Ltd., strategic control
blocks.question: DESCRIBE the process of strategic control and the types of control the chairman should be asking for.
answer_points: **What strategic control is.** It is the process of taking stock of the strategy as it is being implemented — monitoring its progress, assessing the environment in which it is unfolding and correcting course — rather than waiting for the five years to end and counting the result.

**Premise control.** Every strategy is built on assumptions about the environment and the industry. Premise control systematically and continuously checks whether those premises still hold — for Vaigai, the assumed room-rate growth, the assumed occupancy and the assumed cost of a new property. When a premise fails, the strategy must be changed, not pursued harder.

**Strategic surveillance.** A broad, unfocused watch over a range of events inside and outside the company that could affect the strategy — trade press, competitors' announcements, regulatory news. It is deliberately not targeted, because the thing that derails a strategy is usually not on anybody's list.

**Special alert control.** A rapid and thorough reconsideration of the strategy in the light of a sudden, unexpected event — a fire at a property, the collapse of a rival, a new tax. It is handled through a crisis team and a contingency plan.

**Implementation control.** The control the chairman is actually asking for in month three: it reviews whether the strategy should continue in the light of unfolding results, by **monitoring strategic thrusts** (the individual projects and steps that make up the strategy) and by **reviewing milestones** — checkpoints set at particular dates or at the completion of particular events, at which progress is assessed and the commitment of further resources reconsidered.
blocks.conclusion: The chairman should ask for all four, but the one that answers his question in month three is implementation control through milestone review: fix the milestones now, at dates and events in the plan, and make further funding conditional on reaching them.
blocks.marks_split: 1 mark for the process, 1 mark each for the four types of control.
blocks.mistake: Describing operational control instead. Operational control compares actual performance against a standard over a short period; strategic control questions the strategy itself, including the premises it rests on.

blocks.label: Q5(b) — Porter's value chain, primary activities
blocks.question: EXPLAIN the primary activities in Porter's value chain and STATE how a firm uses it to find a source of competitive advantage.
answer_points: **Inbound logistics.** Receiving, storing, handling and distributing the inputs — material handling, warehousing, inventory control, vehicle scheduling and returns to suppliers.
**Operations.** Transforming the inputs into the final product — machining, packaging, assembly, equipment maintenance, testing and printing.
**Outbound logistics.** Storing the finished product and getting it to the buyer — warehousing of finished goods, material handling, delivery vehicle operation, order processing and scheduling.
**Marketing and sales.** Providing the means by which buyers can buy and inducing them to do so — advertising, promotion, the sales force, quoting, channel selection, channel relations and pricing.
**Service.** Enhancing or maintaining the value of the product after it is sold — installation, repair, training, parts supply and product adjustment.

**How the chain is used.** The firm disaggregates itself into these activities and the supporting ones, works out the cost of each and the value each adds to the buyer, and then looks for the activity in which it performs either **more cheaply** or **better** than its rivals. Competitive advantage cannot be seen by looking at the firm as a whole; it lives in a particular activity, or in the **linkages** between activities, and the chain is the tool that makes it visible.
blocks.conclusion: The five primary activities are inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service. The firm finds its advantage by comparing its cost and its performance activity by activity against rivals', and by managing the linkages between activities that rivals cannot easily copy.
blocks.marks_split: ½ mark for naming each of the five with its content (2½), 1 mark for the support activities if mentioned, 1½ marks for how the chain is used to locate advantage.
blocks.mistake: Listing the four support activities — procurement, technology development, human resource management and firm infrastructure — as primary. The question asks for primary activities specifically; naming the support activities separately earns credit, confusing the two does not.

blocks.label: Q5(c) — Tapti Instruments Ltd., core competence
blocks.question: STATE, with reasons, whether the repair network is a core competence of Tapti Instruments Ltd.
answer_points: **The tests.** Prahalad and Hamel hold that a core competence must satisfy three conditions: it provides **competitive advantage** by giving the customer a benefit rivals cannot match; it is **difficult for competitors to imitate**; and it can be **applied widely** — extended to many products, markets or businesses.

**Competitive advantage — satisfied.** Eighteen hours against four days is a benefit the customer feels directly: a machine on the floor instead of idle. For a buyer of industrial instruments, downtime is the cost that matters, so this is advantage of the kind that affects the purchase decision.

**Difficult to imitate — satisfied.** The network is not one thing that can be bought. It is the combination of a forecasting system built over nine years, a trained cadre of 400 engineers produced by the company's own school, and a review culture enforced from the top. A rival can hire engineers or buy software; assembling all three and the nine years of data behind the forecasting is what it cannot do quickly.

**Wide application — satisfied.** An eighteen-hour service capability can be extended to any product the company chooses to sell to the same industrial customers, and the forecasting and the engineer cadre would carry across to a new instrument range or to servicing other manufacturers' equipment.

**The point of the answer.** The competence is not the 400 engineers, nor the software, nor the managing director's review — any of those alone would be a resource. It is the **bundle**, which is why it is hard to copy and why it counts as a competence rather than an asset.
blocks.conclusion: Yes. The repair network satisfies all three tests and is a core competence of Tapti Instruments Ltd. The company should build its strategy around it and resist any cost-cutting that breaks one strand of the bundle.
blocks.marks_split: 2 marks for stating the three tests, 1 mark for applying each to the facts.
blocks.mistake: Answering that it is a core competence because it is Tapti's strength. The marks are in the three named tests applied to the given facts; a general statement about strengths earns at most a mark.
topics: SM Ch 3 §3.4.1 Criteria for building Core Competencies

blocks.label: Q6(a) — electric two-wheelers, five forces
blocks.question: ANALYSE the electric two-wheeler industry using Porter's five forces model.
answer_points: **Threat of new entrants — high.** Four of the eleven manufacturers were founded within the last five years, which is direct evidence that the entry barriers are low: no established brand loyalty, assembly rather than deep manufacturing, and capital available to new ventures. A high threat of entry caps the prices and the margins the incumbents can hold.

**Bargaining power of suppliers — high.** Battery cells, the largest single element of the cost of the vehicle, come from three suppliers worldwide. A concentrated supplier base for a component with no ready substitute lets the suppliers set terms, and the manufacturers' only real responses are long-term contracts, backward integration into cells, or cell chemistries with a wider supply base.

**Bargaining power of buyers — high.** Buyers compare range and price on aggregator websites before they ever enter a showroom. The information asymmetry that once protected the dealer is gone; switching costs are nil and the purchase is a one-off, so buyers can and do push on price.

**Threat of substitutes — high.** Petrol two-wheelers are available at two-thirds of the price and deliver the same core benefit of personal mobility, with a refuelling network that already exists. That substitute puts a ceiling on electric pricing that no amount of competition between the eleven manufacturers can lift.

**Rivalry among existing competitors — intense.** Eleven players in a market in which products differ mainly on specification, buyers are price-sensitive and capacity has been built ahead of demand produces discounting, heavy advertising and short product cycles.
blocks.conclusion: All five forces are adverse, which marks this out as a structurally unattractive industry in which average profitability will be low. A manufacturer that wants to earn a return must change one of the forces for itself — secure cell supply, build a service and charging network that creates switching costs, or occupy a segment the petrol substitute does not serve.
blocks.marks_split: 1 mark for each force, with the mark given for the fact from the scenario that evidences it, not for the name of the force.
blocks.mistake: Describing the five forces in the abstract and never touching the scenario. Each force must be pinned to the fact that evidences it — three suppliers worldwide, four new entrants in five years, two-thirds of the price.
topics: SM Ch 2 §2.5.1 Porter's Five Forces Model

blocks.label: Q6(b) — concentric versus conglomerate diversification
blocks.question: EXPLAIN the difference between concentric and conglomerate diversification with one example of each.
answer_points: **Concentric diversification.** The new business is **related** to the existing one. The firm moves into a product, market or technology that connects to what it already does, so that it can carry across its technology, its distribution, its brand or its customer relationships. The purpose is synergy: the new business is worth more in this firm's hands than in a stranger's.
**Example of concentric diversification.** A manufacturer of toothpaste adding toothbrushes and mouthwash — the same customers, the same retail shelves, the same sales force and the same brand.

**Conglomerate diversification.** The new business is **unrelated** to the existing one — a different product, a different market and a different technology, with no operating link to carry across. The purpose is not synergy but a better use of surplus funds, a spread of risk across unrelated earnings streams, or entry into a sector growing faster than the existing one.
**Example of conglomerate diversification.** A cement manufacturer acquiring a life insurance business — nothing in the cement operation transfers to insurance except capital and management time.

**The real distinction.** It is not the distance between the two industries but whether there is an operating link the firm can exploit. Concentric diversification is justified by synergy and can be judged by whether the synergy materialises; conglomerate diversification is justified by financial logic and carries the higher risk, because the firm competes in an industry whose success factors it does not know.
blocks.conclusion: Concentric diversification enters a related business and is justified by synergy; conglomerate diversification enters an unrelated business and is justified by financial and risk considerations. The test is the presence or absence of an exploitable operating link, not the apparent distance between the two industries.
blocks.marks_split: 2 marks for concentric with its example, 2 for conglomerate with its example, 1 for the basis of the distinction.
blocks.mistake: Giving an example that does not fit — a car maker entering motorcycles is concentric, not conglomerate, however different the two products look to a consumer. Check the example against the synergy test before writing it.
topics: SM Ch 4 §4.2.2.3 Types of Growth / Expansion Strategy

blocks.label: Q7(a) — McKinsey 7S framework
blocks.question: DESCRIBE the McKinsey 7S framework, STATE which elements are hard and which soft, and why the distinction matters in implementation.
answer_points: **Strategy.** The plan the firm has chosen for building and sustaining competitive advantage, and the allocation of resources behind it.
**Structure.** How the organisation is divided and how its parts report — the lines of authority, the grouping of activities and the degree of centralisation.
**Systems.** The formal and informal procedures by which the work is done and measured — planning, budgeting, information, recruitment, appraisal and reward systems.

**Shared values.** The core beliefs, placed at the centre of the framework because the other six are held together by them; what the organisation actually stands for, as against what the mission statement says.
**Style.** The pattern of behaviour of the senior managers — what they attend to, what they tolerate and how they spend their time, which the organisation reads as the real signal of priorities.
**Staff.** The people: how many, of what kind, how recruited, how developed, how deployed and how motivated.
**Skills.** What the organisation, as distinct from the individuals in it, is distinctively good at — the capabilities that survive the departure of any one person.

**Hard and soft.** The **hard** elements are strategy, structure and systems: they can be written down, specified and changed by a decision from the top. The **soft** elements are shared values, style, staff and skills: they cannot be specified, they change slowly, and they are rarely under direct managerial control.

**Why the distinction matters.** Implementation fails because managers change the hard elements and assume the soft ones will follow. A new structure announced on Monday is in place on Monday; the style and the shared values it needs may take two years, and until they arrive the structure does not work. The framework's central claim is that all seven must be **aligned** — a change in any one requires a matching change in the rest.
blocks.conclusion: The 7S framework holds that effective implementation needs all seven elements aligned around shared values. The three hard elements can be changed by decision; the four soft ones must be built, and the gap between the two timescales is where implementation usually fails.
blocks.marks_split: ½ mark for each of the seven elements (3½), 1 mark for the hard-soft classification, ½ mark for the alignment point.
blocks.mistake: Omitting shared values, or treating it as one of seven items in a list rather than the centre the other six connect to. Note also that the soft elements are the four that begin with S-sounds other than strategy, structure and systems — a mnemonic worth having ready.

blocks.label: Q7(b) — elements of a successful turnaround
blocks.question: EXPLAIN the elements of a successful turnaround strategy the board should put in place.
answer_points: **Changes in the top management.** New leadership is usually required: the managers who presided over the decline rarely carry the credibility to reverse it, and a new chief executive signals to staff, lenders and customers that the board has accepted the diagnosis.

**Initial credibility-building actions.** Early, visible wins — a cost cut delivered, a loss-making line closed, a receivable collected — that persuade the stakeholders the turnaround is real before the larger changes are asked for.

**Neutralising external pressures.** Negotiating with the banks, the creditors, the tax authorities and the unions so that the company is given the time it needs. A turnaround that is technically sound fails if a creditor forecloses in month two.

**Identifying quick payoff activities.** Finding the actions that generate cash fastest — disposing of surplus assets, running down excess inventory, tightening collections — to fund the rest of the programme from within.
**Quick cost reductions.** Attacking the controllable costs at once: discretionary spending, overheads, overtime, and the direct costs of the loss-making lines.
**Revenue generation.** Price and volume actions on the lines that do make money, a review of the product mix, and renewed attention to the customers who are worth keeping.
**Asset reduction.** Selling or shutting what the company no longer needs — surplus plant, land, divisions outside the chosen core — to release cash and reduce the fixed cost base.

**Improved internal and external communication.** Telling staff, shareholders, lenders and customers what is being done and why, so that the uncertainty itself does not cause people to leave and customers to switch.
blocks.conclusion: For a company with six quarters of falling sales, a tight cash position and two loss-making lines of four, the sequence matters: credibility and cash first (new management, quick cost cuts, quick payoff activities, external pressures neutralised), then asset reduction and the rebuilding of revenue on the two lines that work.
blocks.marks_split: ½ mark for each of the eight elements, 1 mark for relating the sequence to the facts given.
blocks.mistake: Confusing the **elements** of a turnaround with its **stages** (assessment and evaluation, acute need, restructuring, stabilisation, return to normal growth) or with the **danger signals** that precede it. All three lists are examinable and the question's wording selects one of them.

blocks.label: Q8(a) — strategic alliances
blocks.question: EXPLAIN the advantages a firm obtains from a strategic alliance and STATE three reasons why alliances fail.
answer_points: **Organisational advantages.** The alliance lets a firm learn necessary skills and obtain capabilities from its partner — expertise it would otherwise have to build over years or buy at the price of a whole company.
**Economic advantages.** Costs and risks are shared between the partners, and the combined scale yields economies the partners could not reach alone, in purchasing, production or distribution.

**Strategic advantages.** Rivals can be joined rather than fought, where the two firms' strengths are complementary; and the alliance can open a product, a technology or a market that neither partner could enter unaided.

**Political advantages.** An alliance with a local firm may be the only practicable way into a country whose rules, approvals or distribution are closed to an outsider — and in some jurisdictions a local partner is a legal requirement.
**Why alliances fail — (i) divergent objectives.** The partners want different things from the arrangement, and the difference surfaces only when a decision has to be made that favours one of them.

**Why alliances fail — (ii) unequal contribution and mistrust.** One partner comes to believe it is contributing more than it receives, or that the other is using the alliance to acquire its technology and then leave.

**Why alliances fail — (iii) cultural and managerial incompatibility.** Differences in decision speed, formality, risk appetite and management style make day-to-day working impossible even where the commercial logic is sound. A fourth common cause is the absence of a clear exit arrangement, which turns a disagreement into a deadlock.
blocks.conclusion: The advantages fall into four groups — organisational, economic, strategic and political. Alliances fail where the objectives diverge, where contribution is felt to be unequal and trust goes, or where the two managements cannot work together.
blocks.marks_split: ½ mark for each of the four advantage groups with its content (2), 1 mark for each of the three reasons for failure.
blocks.mistake: Listing advantages without the four-group structure. ICAI's own answer groups them as organisational, economic, strategic and political, and the grouping is what distinguishes a full-mark answer from a half-mark list.

blocks.label: Q8(b) — the GE Stop-Light matrix
blocks.question: DESCRIBE the GE Stop-Light matrix, the prescription for each zone, and the respect in which it improves on BCG.
answer_points: **The two axes.** The vertical axis is **business strength** and the horizontal axis is **industry attractiveness**, each graded high, medium and low, giving a three-by-three grid of nine cells. Both axes are composites: business strength is built from market share, profitability, technological position and brand; industry attractiveness from market size, growth, margins, competitive intensity and regulation.
**The green zone — invest and expand.** The three cells where the business is strong and the industry attractive. These businesses get the money; the company grows them.

**The yellow zone — select and earn.** The diagonal cells of medium overall standing. These businesses are held and managed for earnings, with investment made selectively and only where a specific case can be made.
**The red zone — harvest and divest.** The three cells where the business is weak and the industry unattractive. The company takes what cash it can and exits.

**The improvement on BCG — (i) more than one variable per axis.** BCG reduces the vertical axis to market growth rate and the horizontal to relative market share. GE uses a weighted composite of several factors on each axis, which is a far closer approximation to what makes an industry attractive and a business strong.

**The improvement on BCG — (ii) nine cells instead of four.** The middle grade admits the businesses that are neither clearly strong nor clearly weak — which is most of them — instead of forcing them into one of four corners.
**The improvement on BCG — (iii) a prescription that is not binary.** 'Select and earn' is a real strategic answer for a real category of business; BCG offers only build, hold, harvest or divest.
blocks.conclusion: The GE matrix places each business on composite measures of business strength and industry attractiveness in a nine-cell grid, prescribing invest and expand for the green zone, select and earn for the yellow and harvest or divest for the red. Its advance on BCG is the use of multiple factors on each axis and the admission of a middle category.
blocks.marks_split: 1 mark for the axes and the grid, 1 mark for each of the three zones with its prescription, 1 mark for the comparison with BCG.
blocks.mistake: Reversing the axes. In the GE matrix business strength is the vertical axis and industry attractiveness the horizontal — the opposite of the arrangement most students remember from BCG, where market growth is vertical. Also note the inconsistency in ICAI's own material for low attractiveness with average strength, which is shown in the yellow zone in the diagram and prescribed harvest or divest in the text; state whichever you use and say why.

Kp = preference dividend ÷ market price = 12 ÷ 105 = **11.43%**. (C) is the coupon on face value; (A) wrongly applies a tax shield — a preference dividend is not tax-deductible, which is the whole point of the question.
Kd = interest (1 − t) ÷ market price = 10 × 0.70 ÷ 96 = 7 ÷ 96 = **7.29%**. (A) applies the tax shield but forgets the ₹96 price; (D) forgets the tax.

On book values the equity weight falls from 200/299.6 = 66.8% to 80/180 = 44.4%. Shifting weight away from the costliest source (16%) towards cheaper ones **lowers** the WACC — on book weights it works out to about 12.08%. (C) is the trap: the component costs are indeed unchanged, but the WACC is a weighted average and the weights have changed.

EOQ = √(2AO ÷ C) = √(2 × 40,000 × 100 ÷ 2) = √40,00,000 = **2,000 units**. At the EOQ, ordering cost = 20 orders × ₹100 = ₹2,000 and carrying cost = (2,000 ÷ 2) × ₹2 = ₹2,000, so the total is **₹4,000**. Note that the two are equal at the EOQ — that is the property that defines it. (B) gives only one half of the cost.

Incremental contribution = ₹9,00,000 × 30% = ₹2,70,000. Investment in debtors: present 36,00,000 × 0.70 × 60/360 = ₹4,20,000; proposed 45,00,000 × 0.70 × 90/360 = ₹7,87,500; increase ₹3,67,500, costing ₹3,67,500 × 15% = ₹55,125. Net benefit = 2,70,000 − 55,125 = **₹2,14,875**, so extend the credit. (A) ignores the carrying cost; (D) computes the contribution on sales rather than on the increase.

Under MM, dividend policy is irrelevant: value depends on the firm's **earning power and the risk of its assets**, not on how the earnings are split between dividend and retention. (C) is Walter's and Gordon's position, not MM's.

Growth of 2% a year, flat total volumes, twenty competitors, price-based switching and four years of falling margins is the **maturity** stage. Decline would show a sharp downward drift in sales, which the facts do not.

A product the company has never made (new product) for a market it has never served (new market) is **diversification** — the risky cell, because the firm can rely neither on its product nor on its position in an established market.

A constant percentage fall in unit cost for every doubling of **cumulative** output is the **experience curve**. (A) economies of scale relate cost to the rate of output per period, not to cumulative volume; (C) the learning curve is the narrower, individual-level idea, and the facts describe plant managers and workers together.

Buying the fleet that supplied the company moves it towards the **source of supply**: backward vertical integration. (B) forward would be moving towards the customer — buying a distributor or opening retail.

Fourteen years of spreadsheets, managers telling their supervisors the system will not work, and a declared intention to run the old way in parallel is classic **resistance to change**. The managing director's task is change management — communicating the case, involving the plant managers in the design, training them and showing early results — not reselecting the technology.

The **vision** says what the organisation wants to become; the **mission** says what business it is in, whom it serves and how. (A) reverses them. (C) describes objectives, which are the quantified, time-bound element of strategic intent.

Stability means the firm **stays with the same business and the same product-market posture**. Changing its definition of its business is the opposite of stability — it is expansion or diversification. (A), (B) and (C) are all among ICAI's eight characteristics.

**Cash cows** are held: high relative share in a low-growth market, so the business is milked for cash without further investment to build share. Stars get Build, question marks Build or Divest, dogs Harvest or Divest.

blocks.label: Q1(a) — Vaitarna Plastics Ltd., payback and IRR
blocks.question: COMPUTE the payback period and the IRR, and ADVISE the company.
answer_points: **Payback period.** With an even annual inflow, payback = initial outlay ÷ annual inflow = ₹2,00,000 ÷ ₹60,000 = **3.33 years**, that is 3 years and 4 months.
**The IRR condition.** At the IRR the net present value is nil, so the present value of the annuity must equal the outlay: PVAF × ₹60,000 = ₹2,00,000, which requires a **PVAF of 3.3333**.
**Locating the rate.** The required factor of 3.3333 lies between 3.352 (at 15%) and 3.274 (at 16%), so the IRR is between 15% and 16%.

**Why the annuity shortcut works.** Because the inflow is the same every year, the IRR can be found from a single annuity factor. Where the inflows are uneven, the PVAF route is unavailable and the IRR has to be found by trial discounting each year's flow separately.
blocks.conclusion: Payback 3.33 years; IRR 15.24%. The IRR exceeds the cost of capital of 14%, so the project should be accepted. (At 14% the NPV is also positive — ₹60,000 × 3.433 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹5,980 — which is the same conclusion reached the other way.)
blocks.marks_split: 1 mark for payback, 1 for the PVAF condition, 1 for locating the bracket, 1½ for the interpolation, ½ for the advice.
blocks.mistake: Interpolating the wrong way round, which gives 15.76% instead of 15.24%. Keep the rule in mind: the lower rate gives the **higher** factor, so you add to the lower rate the fraction of the way the required factor has travelled down from it.

blocks.label: Q1(b) — Manjira Foods Ltd., leverage in reverse
blocks.question: COMPUTE EBIT, contribution, sales and fixed cost, and STATE the DCL.
answer_points: **Start from the financial leverage, because it is the only relation with a known rupee figure in it.** DFL = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − Interest) = 1.5, so EBIT = 1.5 (EBIT − ₹2,00,000) → EBIT = 1.5 EBIT − ₹3,00,000 → 0.5 EBIT = ₹3,00,000 → **EBIT = ₹6,00,000**.
**Contribution from the operating leverage.** DOL = Contribution ÷ EBIT = 2, so contribution = 2 × ₹6,00,000 = **₹12,00,000**.
**Sales from the P/V ratio.** Contribution ÷ Sales = 40%, so sales = ₹12,00,000 ÷ 0.40 = **₹30,00,000**.
**Degree of combined leverage.** DOL × DFL = 2 × 1.5 = **3 times**. Check directly: contribution ÷ EBT = 12,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 3. ✓
**Statement of the position.** Sales ₹30,00,000; variable cost ₹18,00,000; contribution ₹12,00,000; fixed cost ₹6,00,000; EBIT ₹6,00,000; interest ₹2,00,000; EBT ₹4,00,000.
blocks.conclusion: EBIT ₹6,00,000; contribution ₹12,00,000; sales ₹30,00,000; fixed cost ₹6,00,000; DCL 3 times. A 1% change in sales will change the pre-tax profit by 3%.

blocks.mistake: Trying to start from the DOL, which has two unknowns in it (contribution and EBIT) and cannot be solved. The DFL is the entry point in every reverse-leverage question because the interest figure anchors it.
